list.listitem: In children, there is no single best tool for assessing severity of exacerbation, monitoring response to treatment or predicting need for hospitalization. Diagnosis in infants should rely on physical exam findings rather than FEV1. C
Early treatment of asthma exacerbations is the best strategy for management and improved outcomes. A

Initial treatment should include oxygen and a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) for all patients; ipratropium bromide, especially for moderate to severe exacerbations; and systemic corticosteroids for most patients. A
Response to initial treatment in the ED is a better predictor of need for hospitalization than severity of the attack on presentation. C
Combined use of a SABA and an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) as a rescue inhaler has been shown to reduce moderate to severe exacerbations compared with SABA alone.A

background.definition: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways. Asthma exacerbation is characterized by worsening wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough due to reversible airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness.

list.listitem: There are almost 183,000 asthma related hospitalizations per year and almost 3,500 asthma related deaths per year.
Asthma affects close to 25 million people in the United States.
Asthma is the most common potentially serious complication in pregnancy.
Acute asthma accounts for 1.5 million emergency room visits per year in the United States, and 14 million lost school days.
It is the third most common reason for hospitalization in those under 15 years of age, and is the most common chronic illness in children.
Allergen exposure in sensitized individuals.
Viral infections.
Exercise.
Irritants.
NSAIDs.
Tobacco smoke.
Non-selective beta blockers.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease.
Use of antibiotics in the first year of life is associated with later development of asthma.
Young children with atopic eczema are at increased risk of asthma—approximately one-third will develop it after the age of 6 years.
Asthma exacerbations vary in severity and duration.
Exacerbations have two phases: Early allergen response (EAR) and the late allergen response (LAR).
Bronchospasm of the EAR involves release of leukotrienes LTC4, LTD4, LTE4.
50% of patients will then produce a TH2 induced LAR about 4 hours after the initial trigger that will usually persist 12 to 24 hours, but in some children may persist for several days.
See chapter on Asthma (chronic management) for a detailed discussion of chronic measures to prevent exacerbations.

Teach patients to monitor signs and symptoms of clinical deterioration so early treatment can be initiated based on an Asthma Action Plan. Evidence for the effectiveness of Asthma Action Plans is equivocal though. C

Patients with asthma should have medications and equipment at home necessary for treating exacerbations. Parent initiated steroids have a small benefit compared with physician controlled prescribing at preventing exacerbations, and may result in more frequent use of steroids. B
Avoid allergen exposure, tobacco smoke (both primary and second hand). B
Influenza vaccine is recommended for patients with asthma to prevent exacerbations, but evidence of benefit is minimal. Influenza vaccine does not worsen asthma. B
Pneumococcal vaccine is also recommended for patients with asthma to prevent exacerbations, but evidence of benefit is minimal. B
Proton pump inhibitors do not prevent asthma exacerbations in adults with concomitant GERD and asthma. B
Probiotics during pregnancy or early in life do not prevent a later diagnosis of asthma.

A short-acting beta agonist (SABA) prior to exercise remains the mainstay of therapy for exercise-induced asthma, to prevent symptoms. Warming or humidifying air and leukotriene inhibitor use may also be helpful.

Vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy (2800 IU/day) does not reduce the risk of wheezing or asthma in children. It also does not reduce the likelihood of asthma exacerbations in children with asthma and low vitamin D levels.
Patients should be instructed to recognize early signs of worsening asthma. C
Diagnosis of an exacerbation in infants should rely on physical exam findings rather than objective measures such as FEV1. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Irreversible airflow obstruction and decreased DLCO
Inspiratory wheezing or stridor, normal lung volumes, normal DLCO
Rales, edema, gallop, decreased ejection fraction on echocardiogram
Unilateral rales, loud pulmonic component of second heart sound
GI complaints, infertility, abnormal sweat chloride test
Unresponsive to bronchodilator or corticosteroid, high resolution CT Scan
Poor response to corticosteroids, pulmonary fibrosis, pH probe monitoring
No diurnal variation, symptoms improve with heliox inhalation
Truncation of inspiratory portion of the flow volume loop, laryngoscopy
Expiratory wheezing, weight loss, high peripheral eosinophilia
Restriction and decreased DLCO on PFTs
Elevated levesl of 5 hydroxyindolacetic acid in the urine

list.listitem: Asthma exacerbations are divided into three categories: mild, moderate, and severe. The peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) correlates well with FEV1 and can easily be performed in the outpatient and inpateint settings when spirometry is not accessible. Mild: initial FEV1 greater than or equal to 200 L/min or greater than or equal to 70% of predicted best. Moderate: initial FEV1 80 to 200 L/min or 40% to 69% of predicted best. Severe: initial FEV1 less than or equal to 80 L/min or less than or equal to 40% of predicted best. "Life threatening" is a sub-set of severe, with an initial FEV1 of less than 25% of predicted best.

The patient with an acute exacerbation of asthma will commonly complain of dyspnea with exercise or at rest, cough, wheezing, and/or chest tightness. The symptoms are usually of rapid onset, i.e., less than 24 hours but may occur over several days.

Description of symptoms may vary by ethnic or socioeconomic group. In one study, African-American patients typically used phrases like "tight throat," "voice tight," "itchy throat," and "tough breath."
Parental report of breathing problems and cough or child reports of noisy breathing, cough, or clogged breathing are good predictors of asthma.
Absence of breathing problems and cough is strong evidence against asthma in a child.
In adults, cough with wheezing is the most sensitive finding, while self-reported or doctor diagnosed asthma are most specific.
Vital signs may include fever, tachycardia, tachypnea or hypotension in severe exacerbations. They may be normal in mild exacerbations.
Physical exam findings may include an audible wheeze and/or decreased airflow on expiration.
Severe attacks may present with cyanosis, use of accessory muslces of respiration, and a pulsus paradoxus greater than 10 mm Hg. The patient may appear restless, agitated, or diaphoretic.
Observations in infants include grunting, retractions and flaring.

Chest radiographs tend not to alter care in acute exacerbations of asthma and most commonly reveal hyperinflation. A CXR should be ordered only in those patients with evidence of complications such as leukocytosis, hypoxemia, unexplained chest pain, or temperature >38.3°C.

Use of continuous pulse oximetry can be used at anytime during asthma attacks, but particularly in patients in severe distress with an FEV1 or PEFR less than 40 percent of their baseline or if they are unable to perform measures of lung function. A post-treatment oxygen saturation <91% increases the likelihood of an unfavorable outcome.
ABG testing is indicated in patients with persistent dyspnea despite bronchodilator therapy who have a peak expiratory flow below 25 percent of normal.

A PEFR can be used to monitor a patient's response to treatment if used over time and can be used in any patient experiencing an exacerbation of symptoms. A PEFR below 200 L/min is an indication of severe obstruction. A major limitation of PEFR is effort and results may vary among individuals by 30%. Routine measurement of PEFR does not help predict subsequent exacerbations.
Pulmonary function tests with spirometry and flow volume loops is typically used in the non-decompensated state.

Exhaled nitric oxide (NO) levels can be used to diagnose asthma. Values over 14 ppb (and especially over 20 ppb) are strong evidence in favor of the diagnosis of asthma, while values <10 ppb significantly reduce the likelihood.
A clinical prediction rule to predict relapse within 8 weeks of an asthma exacerbation in adults has been developed and successfully validated.

The likelihood that a child will require hospitalization can be predicted by a validated clinical decision rule. Key variables include age <6 years, male gender, severity of pretreatment wheeze, whether oxygen was required, and post-treatment oxygen saturation.
The Pediatric Respiratory Assessment Measure (PRAM) score at 3 hours predicts the need for hospitalization.
Normal values for peak flow are shown here.
Treatment of an asthma exacerbation progresses step wise according to degree. See .
Short-acting beta-agonists (SABA) are the treatment of choice for treating acute asthma symptoms and exacerbations. A
Combined use of a SABA and an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) as a rescue inhaler has been shown to reduce moderate to severe exacerbations compared with SABA alone.A
Systemic corticosteroids significantly reduce the frequency of relapse, need for hospitalization, and requirement for increased use of SABA. A
Initial treatment should include oxygen and a SABA for all patients; ipratropium bromide, especially for moderate to severe exacerbations; and systemic corticosteroids for most patients. A
For severe exacerbations that do not respond to initial treatment consider IV magnesium or heliox.,,B
See for an overview of drug treatment of acute asthma exacerbations.
A randomized trial found that hospital at home for conditions such as asthma saved money with equally good outcomes and less likelihood of 30 day readmission.

listitem.strong: Inhaled short-acting beta-agonists, anticholinergics, and corticosteroids

list.listitem: Short acting beta2 agonists (SABA) are recommended for all patients. Adverse effects include hypokalemia, muscle tremor, tachycardia, and increased lactic acid. Levalbuterol (Xopenex) is no more effective nor safer than albuterol in children with moderate asthma exacerbations. There is no benefit to nebulizers over MDIs in adults and cooperative children, especially when spacers are used. Homemade spacers using plastic bottles are even effective. A Cochrane review found that continuous administration of a SABA (at least every 15 minutes) was more effective at preventing hospitalization than intermittent administration in 8 studies with 461 patients (RR 0.68; 95% CI 0.5-0.9). Continuous treatment was not associated with significant differences in blood pressure, heart rate or adverse effects.

Inhaled ipratroprium bromide is recommended for patients with moderate to severe exacerbations in the emergency department. Patients receiving ipratropium bromide have a modest improvement in airflow obstruction when used in conjunction with a beta-2 agonist. A Cochrane review found 20 trials with 2697 children comparing SABA plus anticholinergic (e.g., ipratropium) to SABA alone. They found that adding the anticholinergic significantly reduced the likelihood of hospital admission (RR 0.73; 95% CI 0.63-0.85, absolute reduction 17 vs 23 out of 100 children), and that this benefit was somewhat greater as the severity of the exacerbation increased. Adverse effects include dry mouth and respiratory secretions.

Adding nebulized budesonide to standard therapy (SABA, ipratropium, and oral steroids) in children with moderate to severe exacerbations did not improve outcomes in a well-designed and adequately powered study. Although evidence supporting a benefit is uncertain, inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) should be considered for patients upon discharge from the ED or hospital setting.They are not a substitute for systemic corticosteroids in moderate or severe exacerbations.

In young children with a history of wheeze during respiratory infection, pre-emptive treatment with a nebulized steroid during a subsequent respiratory tract infection does not prevent a second episode of wheeze or decrease the duration of symptoms.

A systematic review of 16 RCTs and 3 non-randomized studies found that albuterol given via nebulizer or MDI with spacer was effective in children younger than 6 years with acute asthma. The review found reasonable evidence that children younger than 6 years have improved clinical scores, respiratory rates, and oxygen saturation after treatment with a SABA.

A systematic review identified 24 studies with 2025 children that reported safety of albuterol. While adverse events were more common in children receiving albuterol (odds ratio 2.1, 95% CI 0.69 to 6.5) this difference was not significant. Nebulized albuterol did cause significantly more adverse events than control (6.4% vs 1.2%, OR 6.76; 2.01 - 22.7).

The FAST trial randomized 1922 adults with asthma to a usual care strategy for exacerbations or to a temporary quadrupling of the inhaled corticosteroid dose. The latter strategy saved money and was more effective.

listitem.em: Combined steroid + SABA as rescue inhaler

list.listitem: Several studies have compared combined use of a SABA and an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) as a rescue inhaler with SABA alone. A study in 1201 Black and Hispanic adults with moderate to severe, poorly controlled asthma randomized them to SABA alone or adding an 80 mcg puff of beclomethasone for each puff of the SABA. There was approximately one fewer exacerbation for every 8 patients using teh combined rescue inhaler.

Another study randomized 3132 patients 4 years and older (mean age 49 years, 6% less than 18) to receive 1 of 3 types of rescue inhaler, each given as 2 actuations (doses shown are per actuation): (1) albuterol 90 mcg plus budesonide 80 mcg, (2) albuterol 90 mcg plus budesonide 40 mcg, or (3) albuterol 90 mcg. Patients in the higher-dose budesonide group had significantly fewer severe exacerbations than those in the albuterol-only group (hazard ratio [HR] 0.74; 95% CI 0.62 - 0.89). There were also fewer severe exacerbations in the low-dose budesonide group than in the albuterol-only group, but this difference was smaller and not statistically significant (HR 0.84; 0.71 - 1.0).

A study randomized 2516 persons 12 and older with poorly controlled mild asthma to SBA alone or SABA + budesonide 160 mcg for acute exacerbations. They found that a combination reduced severe exacerbations (5.3% vs 9.4%, NNT = 26).
Systemic corticosteroids are recommended for all patients with moderate to severe exacerbations and any patient who does not respond completely to SABA.
An RCT found that 3 days of oral corticosteroids was effective as 5 days in children discharged from the ED following an exacerbation (using 1 mg/kg oral prednisolone).
Even in hospitalized children, oral steroids are similar to IV in effectiveness.

A systematic review and a more recent large RCT with 557 patients found that in children with acute asthma exacerbation, 1 or 2 IM doses of dexamethasone were similarly effective to 5 days of oral prednisone or prednisolone.
A network meta-analysis of 11 RCTs with 2353 children found that all oral corticosteroids were similar effective for treatment of acute asthma exacerbation in children.

A study in adults with mild to moderate asthma exacerbation (n = 257) randomized them to 2 days of dexamethasone 16 mg daily or 5 days of prednisone 60 mg daily, and found faster return to usual activities in the dexamethasone group, with no other differences in outcomes.

In another study, 456 adults with an acute asthma exacerbation were randomized to a single dose of dexamethasone 12 mg or 5 days of oral prednisone 60 mg once daily. The risk of relapse was slightly higher in the dexamethasone group (12.1% vs 9.8%) and did not meet the prespecified criteria for non-inferioirity.

A randomized trial of 199 adults with an acute asthma exacerbation who had not had an antibiotic in the previous month randomized them to azithromycin 500 mg daily or placebo for 3 days. No differences between groups in outcomes were seen, although the trial was somewhat underpowered.

For children age 12 to 72 months with recurrent wheeze associated respiratory illness (WARI; severe wheezing in the context of a lower RTI that required systemic steroids), oral azithromycin 12 mg/kg once daily at the beginning of an episode reduced the likelihood that it would progress to a severe lower respiratory tract infection (HR 0.64; 95% CI 0.41-0.98). The benefit was greater in those with more previous RTIs (NNT = 33 for 1, NNT = 14 for 2, and NNT = 7 for 4).

A Cochrane review identified 6 studies with 681 adults and children comparing antibiotics with placebo or usual care in persons with an acute asthma exacerbation who did not have a clear indication (such as a radiographic infiltrate) for antibiotics. The authors concluded that there is limited quality evidence to support a modest benefit of antibiotics, but that they were too inconsistent and studies were too heterogeneous to draw any clear conclusions.

A study using an administrative database with 543 hospitals compared patients hospitalized for an acute exacerbation of asthma treated with an antibiotic with those not receiving an antibiotic, using propensity score matching. Use of an antibiotic was associated with a longer hospital stay, higher costs, more diarrhea, and no effect on asthma outcomes otherwise.
IV magnesium sulfate may be useful in patients with impending respiratory failure and should be considered for those who fail to respond within one hour of initial treatment.

A systematic review identified 11 randomized comparing IV MgSO4 with placebo. In 4 studies they found a reduction in hospitalizaitons (OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.03-0.73), while 2 studies found some improvements in lung function.

One study found that nebulized magnesium sulfate was also effective. Another study of 248 patients with severe acute asthma found small improvements in lung function at 4 hours but no change in hospitalization rates or other outcomes.
A randomized trial of 818 children with refractory acute asthma found no benefit to adding nebulized magnesium to albuterol.

A systematic review found 10 randomized trials with 2301 children given nebulized MgSO4 or placebo and salbutamol. They found no difference in hospitalization, need for ICU admission, or length of stay.

A Cochrane review of 25 trials with nearly 3000 patients concluded that there are some modest additional benefits of nebulized MgSO4 when added to other bronchodilators, although the trials were heterogeneous. It did appear to be safe, and patients with more severe disease may experience greater benefit.

Systemic beta-2 agonists: Systemic beta-2 agonists such as epinephrine or terbutaline are sometimes given for severe exacerbations. While some studies have found a benefit of IV albuterol, a systematic review found no strong evidence of benefit based on several small, low-quality studies.
Heliox: Heliox driven albuterol nebulization should be considered for those patients who remain in the severe category after one hour of initial treatment.

Leukotriene inhibitors: The use of montelukast can reduce mild, moderate, and part of severe exacerbations in chronic mild to moderate asthma. In comparison with placebo, adults with chronic asthma receiving montelukast had reduced number or exacerbations (OR = 00.60 and 95% CI, 0.49, 0.74; NNT = 17 and 95% CI, 12, 29) and its use in acute asthma can improve peak expiratory flow percent predicted (p = 0.008) and systemic corticosteroid intake (p = 0.005). High dose zafirlukast (160 mg on arrival in ED) slightly reduced the number of patients with an extended hospital stay. A comparison of prednisolone with montelukast in children discharged from the ED following an acute exacerbation found that steroids were more effective (NNT = 7 for treatment failure).
A Cochrane review conclude that methylxanthines (aminophylline), mucolytics, and chest physiotherapy do not appear to be effective based on current best evidence.
Homeopathy, air ionizers, manual therapy, and acupuncture have been used for treatment of asthma but evidence of benefit of is lacking. C

Antioxidant dietary supplementation, including natural anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory agents, may have a role in asthma management, but there is no clinical trial data to support their use. Vitamin D does not prevent asthma exacerbations in vitamin D deficient individuals.
There is insufficient evidence to support the use of relaxation techniques and yoga for asthma exacerbation.
Efficacy and safety of herbal treatments for asthma is unknown.
A randomized trial with 386 asthma patients found no benefit for soy supplementation.
A small study found a small, non-clinically significant in sleep quality using melatonin in women with mild/moderate asthma.
Breathing retraining techniques may result in a reduced use of rescue bronchdilators and decreased frequency of asthma exacerbations.
Oxygen is recommended for most patients except those with mild exacerbation.

Patients presenting with apnea or coma should be intubated immediately. There are no other absolute indications to intubate for asthma exacerbation. Al soconsider intubation in patients with persistent or increasing hypercapnia, exhaustion, or depression of mental status.

While widely used clinically, there are only limited and inconclusive data regarding the efficacy of non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) for patients with impending respiratory failure due to a severe asthma exacerbation. A Cochrane review found only 3 RCTs with 60 children and while there was a large reduction in the need for intubation (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.95) the confidence interval was wide and study quality poor.
A Cochrane review found that caffeine improves lung function for up to 2 hours after consumption, based on 7 tiny studies with a total of 75 people.

A Cochrane review concluded that educational interventions for asthma patients in the ED reduce the likelihood of subsequent hospital admissions (RR 0.5; 95% CI 0.27-0.91). Patient education interventions in the ED can also increase the likelihood that the patient follows up with their primary care physician.
An updated meta-analysis (2022) also found that asthma education reduces hospitalizations (RR 0.46; 95% CI 0.32 - 0.66) and ED visits (RR 0.69; 0.59 - 0.81) in children.
Longer stay in a special emergency department "step-up" unit specializing in asthma care can improve clinical outcomes and reduce costs.

Consider referral when response to treatment is slow, intermittent or incomplete; when quality of life is affected; when the patient requires frequent visits to the emergency room for treatment; when consideration is being given to immunotherapy; for patients who experience sudden severe asthma attacks; patients with persistent nocturnal asthma; patients who require frequent burst of systemic corticosteroids.

The decision to hospitalize a patient with an acute exacerbation is based on multiple factors such as duration and severity of symptoms, degree of airflow obstruction, response to treatment in the ED, response of prior exacerbations, access to health care.
A validated clinical rule predicts the likelihood a child will need hospitalization.
See chapter on pneumothorax for its management.
Respiratory failure is the most dire complication, requiring mechanical ventilation.
Asthma education has been shown to reduce readmissions in adults and in adolescents.
Patients hospitalized with exacerbations of asthma should continue to be treated with SABA to relieve airflow obstruction.
Systemic corticosteroids should be given and continued unil FEV1 returns to >70% of predicted or personal best.
Consideration should be given to initiating inhaled corticosteroids prior to discharge from the hospital.
Medical follow up should be scheduled for 1 to 4 weeks after discharge. Patients should receive a written care plan for recognizing signs of acute decompensation upon discharge.
Asthma exacerbations that are recognized and treated within 6 hours of onset are less likely to require hospitalization. C
Medical follow up should take place 1 to 4 weeks after treatment for the acute exacerbation and/or discharge from the ED/hospital. B
A validated clinical rule can predict the likelihood of relapse in adults.
A post-treatment oxygen saturation <91% increases the likelihood of an unfavorable outcome.
Continue treatment with inhaled SABA after release from ED/hospital. Patient should be instructed to call physician if using >12 puffs in 24 hours.
Continue oral corticosteroids until FEV1 is stable at 70% of predicted or personal best.
After an acute exacerbation patients should receive follow up care within 1 to 4 weeks.
There is insufficient evidence that using a written action plan based on peak flow and/or FEV1 alters outcomes compared to management based on symptoms alone.
Patients/parents should seek medical help early especially when the exacerbation is severe.
Seek medical help if the patient does not experience rapid, sustained improvement from home treatment.
Asthma is frequently overlooked in the elderly.
Clinical signs and symptoms are similar in the elderly to younger adults.
Airflow obstruction is at least partially reversible, however fixed airflow obstruction is more commonly found in the elderly.
Elderly patients with asthma tend to have lower IgE levels.
Albuterol is the preferred short acting beta agonist in pregnancy.
Budesonide is the preferred inhaled corticosteroid in pregnancy.

A study using pharmacy and clinical databases in Canada found no difference in congenital malformations between women using a long-acting beta-agonist plus an inhlaed corticosteroid versus higher doses of an inhaled corticosteroid.

Assessment in infants should depend on physical exam rather than objective measure such as FEV1. Look for use of accessory muscles, inspiratory and expiratory wheezes, paradoxical breathing, cyanosis, or respiratory rate >60/minute.
Oxygen saturation (SaO2) <90% indicates serious distress.

Infants are at greater risk for respiratory failure, therefore lack of improvement on physical exam or SaO2 level indicate need for hospitalization. A clinical rule can predict need for hospitalization.
Early use of oral corticosteroids is essential to treatment.

Most acute exacerbations are from viral respiratory infections and do not require treatment with antibiotics. A randomized trial of 79 children with an initial episode of wheeze associated with rhinovirus infection found greater short-term benefit with prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day given in two divided doses for 3 days compared with placebo, but no difference in long-term outcomes.

reference.title: clinical practice guideline
Chronic asthma (AHRQ)

cell.label: Assess severity of attack (mild, moderate, or severe), then give nebulized or aerosol beta-2 agonist in multiple doses or continuously.
Arrange follow up; maintains response 60 minutes after last treatment; normal physical exam; consider oral steroids.
Discharge home; continue treatment with inhaled SABA; consider oral steroids; inhaled corticosteroid; patient education; schedule follow-up appt 1-4 weeks.
Consider admission to ward; oxygen; continue inhaled SABA + ipratropium bromide; oral or IV steroids; monitor vital signs, FEV1, SaO2.
PEF ≤50% predicted, pCO2 ≥42 mm Hg, drowsiness or confusion: admit to MICU; O2; inhaled SABA hourly or continuously; consider adjunctive treatment; consider intubation and mechanical ventilation.

footnotes.footnote: PEF, peak expiratory flow; SABA, short-acting beta agonist.
Adapted from the National Heart, Blood, and Lung Institute Expert Panel Report 3 (EPR 3): Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Asthma. NIH Publication no. 08-4051, 2007.

Medication Child Dose Adult Dose
Short-Acting Beta Agonist
(1) Albuterol
Nebulizer solution 0.15 mg/kg every 20 minutes for 3 doses 2.5-5.0 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses
Initial dose
Subsequent doses 0.15-0.3 mg/kg up to 10 mg every 1-4 hours prn or 0.5 mg/kg/hr via continuous nebulization 2.5-10.0 mg every 1-4 hours as needed or 10-15 mg/hr via continuous nebulization
MDI 90 mcg/puff 4-8 puffs every 20 minutes times 3 doses; add valved holding chamber. In children <4 yr use mask 4-8 puffs every 20 minutes up to 4 hours
Initial dose
Subsequent doses Every 1-4 hours prn Every 4 hours prn
(2) Levalbuterol
(R-Albuterol)
Nebulizer solution
Initial dose 0.075 mg/kg (minimum dose 1.25 mg) every 20 minutes for 3 doses 1.25-2.5 mg up to 5 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses
Subsequent doses 0.75-0.15 mg/kg up to 5 mg every 1-4 hours prn 1.25-5.0 mg every 1-4 hours prn
MDI 45 mcg/puff Same as albuterol dosing Same as albuterol dosing
Anticholinergics
Ipratropium bromide
Nebulizer solution
Initial dose 0.25-0.5 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses 0.5 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses
Subsequent doses Repeat as needed Repeat as needed
MDI 18 mcg/puff
Initial dose 4-8 puffs every 20 minutes for 3 doses, add valved holding chamber 8 puffs every 20 minutes for 3 doses
Systemic Beta-2 Agonists
(1) Epinephrine
1:1,000 (1 mg/kg) 0.01 mg/kg SC up to 0.3-0.5 mg every 20 minutes for up to 3 doses 0.3-0.5 mg SC every 20 minutes for up to 3 doses
(2) Terbutaline 1 mg/ml
Initial dose 0.01 mg/kg SC every 20 minutes up to 3 doses 0.25 mg SC every 20 minutes for up to 3 doses
Subsequent doses 0.01 mg/kg SC every 2-6 hours prn
Systemic corticosteroids
Prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg in 2 divided doses with maximum of 60 mg/day continue until FEV1 is 70% of predicted or personal best 40-80 mg in 1-2 doses until FEV1 is 70% of predicted or personal best
Magnesium sulfate 25-75 mg/kg up to 2 g IV 2 g IV
